The isolation number of a tree grows essentially with the number of vertices: for any tree \(T\) one has \(\iota(T)=\big\lfloor \frac{|V(T)|}{3}\big\rfloor\) (the extremal trees are “spiders’’ and paths).  
Subdividing an edge adds exactly one new vertex, so each subdivision can increase \(|V|\) by 1 and can raise \(\iota\) by at most one when the total vertex count passes a multiple of 3.  

Therefore, to force \(\iota\) to increase by 1 we must add enough vertices to move from a size that is a multiple of 3 to the next multiple of 3, which requires at most three new vertices. Because each subdivision contributes one vertex, the minimal number of edges that must be subdivided is at most three.  

There exist trees (e.g., a path with \(|V|\equiv 0\pmod 3\)) for which exactly three subdivisions are needed, so the bound is tight.

\[
\boxed{3}
